intro: Quadratics are equations with an x squared in them; their graphs are U-shaped curves called parabolas. This branch covers graphing them, solving them in several ways, and using them for real problems like the path of a thrown ball.

IV.7.01.what: Identifying the key features of a parabola: its tip (vertex), its mirror line, which way it opens, and where it crosses the axes.

levels.a: Finds the vertex, the lowest or highest point of the U.
levels.b: Finds the vertical mirror line through the vertex.
levels.c: Tells whether the U opens upward or downward.
levels.d: Finds where the parabola crosses the x-axis and the y-axis.

IV.7.02.what: Graphing a quadratic written in vertex form, which shows the tip of the U directly.

levels.a: Reads the vertex straight from the equation.
levels.b: Explains how the number in front makes the U narrower, wider or upside down.
levels.c: Uses the mirror line to find matching points on each side.
levels.d: Picks the correct sketch of the parabola.
levels.e: Finds the vertex when there is a number multiplying x inside the bracket.
levels.f: Finds the lowest vertex among a whole family of changing parabolas.

IV.7.03.what: Graphing a quadratic written in standard form, x squared terms first, then x, then a plain number.

levels.a: Uses a short formula to find the x-position of the vertex.
levels.c: Reads where the curve crosses the y-axis from the plain number.

IV.7.04.what: Graphing a quadratic written in factored form, as brackets multiplied together, which shows the x-axis crossings directly.

levels.a: Reads where the curve crosses the x-axis from the brackets.
levels.b: Finds the vertex halfway between those crossings.
levels.c: Tells from the number in front whether the U opens up or down.

IV.7.05.what: Switching a quadratic between vertex, standard and factored forms.

levels.a: Multiplies out vertex form into standard form.
levels.b: Multiplies out factored form into standard form.
levels.d: Knows which form shows the vertex, the crossings or the y-intercept best.

IV.7.06.what: Solving quadratics by getting the squared part alone and taking the square root of both sides.

levels.a: Gets x squared alone on one side.
levels.b: Takes the square root, remembering both the positive and negative answers.
levels.c: Solves when a whole bracket is squared.
levels.d: Recognizes when there is no real solution, since no square is negative.

IV.7.07.what: Solving a squared equation (a quadratic) by splitting it into two simpler pieces that multiply to zero.

levels.a: Rearranges the equation so one side is zero.
levels.b: Factors the quadratic into two brackets.
levels.c: Solves by setting each bracket to zero, since a product is zero only if a piece is.
levels.d: Checks each answer in the original equation.
levels.e: Expands and tidies a messier equation before factoring.
levels.f: Spots a quadratic in disguise, such as an equation in x to the fourth power, and finds all solutions.

IV.7.08.what: Completing the square: adding the right number to make a perfect squared bracket, which lets any quadratic be solved.

levels.a: Finds the number that completes the square: half the x number, squared.
levels.b: Adds that number to both sides to keep the equation balanced.
levels.c: Does the same when there is a number in front of the x squared.
levels.d: Solves a quadratic fully by completing the square.
levels.e: Handles odd middle numbers, where fractions appear.
levels.f: Completes two squares at once, in x and in y, to find a smallest value.

IV.7.09.what: Using completing the square to rewrite a quadratic in vertex form and find its tip.

levels.a: Groups the x terms and takes out any number in front.
levels.b: Completes the square inside the bracket.
levels.c: Adjusts the plain number so the expression stays the same.
levels.e: Finds a vertex that has fractions in it.
levels.f: Pairs up four brackets cleverly to find the smallest value of a product.

IV.7.10.what: Using the quadratic formula, a recipe that solves any quadratic from its three numbers a, b and c.

levels.a: Identifies the three numbers a, b and c in the equation.
levels.b: Puts them into the formula carefully, starting with the part under the root.
levels.c: Solves and simplifies the square root in the answer.
levels.d: Rearranges the equation into the usual form first, then uses the formula.
levels.e: Works backwards from the answers to find the original equation.
levels.f: Uses the formula when the equation itself contains square roots.

IV.7.11.what: Using the discriminant, the part under the root in the formula, to tell how many solutions a quadratic has without solving.

levels.a: Calculates b squared minus 4 times a times c.
levels.b: Uses its sign to say whether there are two, one or no real solutions.
levels.c: Tells whether the solutions are whole or fraction numbers, or messy roots.
levels.d: Links the discriminant to how many times the graph crosses the x-axis.
levels.e: Finds the missing number that gives exactly one solution.
levels.f: Finds when an equation with an unknown throughout has a repeated solution.

IV.7.12.what: Choosing the quickest way to solve a given quadratic: square roots, factoring or the formula.

levels.a: Uses square roots when there is no plain x term.
levels.b: Checks whether an expression factors neatly.
levels.c: Uses the formula, which always works, when nothing else is quick.
levels.d: Gives a reason for the chosen method.

IV.7.13.what: Using quadratics to model something thrown or launched, whose height rises then falls.

levels.a: Uses the height formula to find the height at a given time.
levels.b: Finds the highest point the object reaches.
levels.c: Finds when the object lands, at height zero.
levels.d: Finds the two times when it passes a given height, going up and coming down.

IV.7.14.what: Using the vertex of a parabola to find the biggest area or best value in real problems.

levels.a: Writes an area as a quadratic expression.
levels.b: Finds the vertex to locate the best value.
levels.c: Finds the largest area or revenue possible, such as for a fenced pen.
levels.d: Explains what the vertex means in the situation.

IV.7.15.what: Solving quadratic inequalities, finding the range of x where a squared expression is above or below zero.

levels.a: Finds where the expression equals zero.
levels.b: Tests the sign in each region between those points.
levels.c: Reads the answer from the graph of the parabola.
levels.d: Writes the answer as ranges in bracket form.
levels.e: Rearranges the inequality first so one side is zero.
levels.f: Finds when an expression is negative for at least one x.

IV.7.16.what: Writing the equation of a parabola from information about it, such as its tip or crossing points.

levels.a: Writes the equation from the vertex and one other point.
levels.b: Writes it from the two x-axis crossings and another point.
levels.c: Writes it from any three points by solving a system.
levels.d: Matches an equation to a graph as a check.
levels.e: Writes it from the mirror line and two points.
levels.f: Finds every parabola that just touches the x-axis and passes through two points.

IV.7.17.what: Fitting a quadratic to data, and recognizing quadratic patterns in tables of numbers.

levels.a: Tells whether a table grows steadily or follows a curved pattern.
levels.b: Finds the differences of the differences, which stay constant for a quadratic.
levels.c: Uses a calculator to fit a quadratic to data.
levels.d: Judges whether a prediction far beyond the data is sensible.
